title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 computed as 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = 2*(1/16) = 0.125. An exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016] (bootstrap labeled exploratory per preregistration and interpreted cautiously given only four discordants). Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, provide execution accounting and representative validator traces, and give explicit artifact pointers and verified hashes for reproducibility.

sections.introduction: Operator intent→device configuration translation can reduce manual effort, but errors in generated CLI sequences or transient unsafe states can cause outages. Modern large language models (LLMs) show promise for translating human intent to device configuration, yet hallucination and factual errors remain central reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow and policy rules, and, if verification fails, run a bounded automated repair attempt. This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment that asks: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? We contribute: (1) a preregistered paired trial (N=500 paired intents) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded description of generation, verifier semantics, and the bounded repair loop; (3) reconciled confirmatory inference (two‑sided conditional exact McNemar) and exploratory paired bootstrap CI descriptions with an explicit small‑discordant‑count caveat; and (4) execution accounting, representative validator traces, and a discussion of verifier blind spots and practical external‑validity limits.
sections.related_work: Existing surveys and system papers demonstrate active interest in LLM‑assisted NetOps: intent translation, intent assurance, AIOps, and multi‑agent orchestration frameworks. Methodological work on RAG/tool‑augmented LLMs and generate–validate–repair advocates combining probabilistic generation with deterministic or domain tools to reduce hallucination risk. Deterministic configuration verifiers (Batfish‑style analyzers and distributed verifier designs) provide feasible oracles for many syntactic and workflow correctness properties. Prior work rarely provides preregistered paired trials with full archival artifacts; this study situates itself at that intersection and follows recommended evaluation practices for tool‑augmented LLM systems.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan: The study was preregistered as study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29 (preregistration SHA‑256 = aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 distinct intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). Sampling seeds, the deterministic task generator, and the analysis executor were frozen before execution. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was pre‑specified as exploratory.
Generation and orchestration: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in execution/model_configuration.json; model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with the deterministic verifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5. If verification failed, the controller invoked at most one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Provider‑call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json and execution manifest) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 with stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 500, repair: 4} and completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 504.
Deterministic verifier semantics and codebook: The primary verifier implements a deterministic validation pipeline on a normalized CLI sequence: (i) syntactic parsing/normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome and the verifier emits structured fields including normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list, and valid (boolean). The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → short description) is archived as an artifact and enumerated in the execution manifest (see execution/execution_manifest.json for the manifest entry that references the verifier codebook artifact). Representative verifier_trace JSON objects are archived under execution/scoring/ and include both validation_before and validation_after objects for each episode.
Repair policy and prompt semantics: The automated repair prompt is constrained: it includes (a) the original intent abstraction, (b) the verifier violation codes and short descriptions, and (c) a request for a canonical corrected CLI sequence. Repairs were limited to a single attempt to bound model‑call costs. A repair candidate is accepted only if the verifier returns valid=true for that subsequent candidate; repair invocation and acceptance are logged per episode in execution/scoring/.
Exact McNemar implementation: The confirmatory test used the conditional exact McNemar formulation that treats discordant pairs only. Let n10 denote pairs where guarded succeeded and baseline failed, and n01 the opposite. With n = n10 + n01 and k = n10, the two‑sided exact conditional p‑value is computed as p = 2 * sum_{x=k}^{n} Binom(n,x) * 0.5^n. For our observed contingency (n10 = 4, n01 = 0 => n = 4, k = 4) this reduces to p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. This is the preregistered decision rule.
sections.results:
Execution and primary counts: The run completed completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions) with model_calls_used = 504. analysis/condition_summary.csv (archived hash: f3e197425cc03dec41cda77f078f6d0b079b06bbde7ac736de5fe988b027ac58) reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; archived hash: 8fb135cec541cbe0b14f16125db33154a41460c49958427fe8e7f3e1f2abfece) is: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked for four initial candidates; all four repair attempts yielded subsequent verifier passes and correspond to n10 = 4. Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008.
Confirmatory exact McNemar calculation: Observed discordants n = 4 with k = 4. Using the conditional binomial formula above yields p = 0.125; because this exact conditional test was preregistered as the decision rule, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance for the primary estimand. The exact contingency CSV and analysis log are archived (paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 8fb135cec541cbe0b14f16125db33154a41460c49958427fe8e7f3e1f2abfece; analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = 261ec80ea9343fccbcd0a62294f5382773770fd59d387dc9d749de50ca909b3e).
Exploratory bootstrap interval and its caveat: The preregistered exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016]; bootstrap artifacts are archived (analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). We emphasize the bootstrap interval was predeclared exploratory: bootstrap percentile intervals resample paired outcomes without conditioning on observed marginal totals, so with near‑ceiling margins and very few discordant pairs a bootstrap interval can exclude zero even when the conditional McNemar is non‑significant. With n=4 discordants the exact conditional test conditions on the margins and yields the preregistered p=0.125; readers should interpret the bootstrap CI as descriptive evidence of a small positive paired difference rather than as a confirmatory result.
Representative artifacts and diagnostics: Representative scoring JSON objects (execution/scoring/task-00000*-*.json) show verifier_trace entries with validation_before, validation_after, normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and validator_version = 5.0. Example episodes covering medium and hard difficulty patterns (shutdown_configure_restore; make_before_break_uplink_switchover; paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) are archived and referenced in the representative_tasks list. The four repaired episodes show verifier‑detectable sequence or availability violations that the single constrained repair prompt corrected; these episodes are identifiable in execution/scoring/ by pair_id and include the repair_provider_trace entries.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and reconciliation: The GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable hazards that baseline would have accepted. The preregistered conditional McNemar (p = 0.125) does not reach confirmatory significance; the exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but must be interpreted cautiously because bootstrap percentile intervals have degraded frequentist coverage under small‑discordant counts. Our analysis follows the preregistration: the exact conditional McNemar is the inferential decision rule, and the bootstrap interval is a predeclared descriptive supplement.
Verifier coverage and blind spots: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency rules, and final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. It does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing or convergence effects, hardware resource exhaustion, or vendor idiosyncrasies. Passing this verifier is necessary for experiment safety in the defined task abstractions but not sufficient for all production hazards; expanding verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators) is required for production automation.
Operational cost and repair rate: Provider audit in deterministic_reconciliation.json records hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 500, repair: 4}. The observed repair invocation rate (4/500) implies modest model‑call overhead for the bounded repair policy in this synthetic workload; workloads with higher hallucination or adversarial input rates would shift this cost/benefit tradeoff. Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008 quantifies marginal generation overhead.
Threats to validity: Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, fixed seeds, and complete pairs (complete_pair_count = 500; no failed episodes). Construct validity is limited by synthetic device templates (synthetic_topologies_v1, synthetic_device_configs_v1) and verifier abstractions. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication and real vendor CLI testing remain future work. Conclusion validity was affected by observed margins: the preregistered power plan assumed a larger baseline discordance (target effect ≈ 0.08), but the realized near‑ceiling baseline (0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, reducing realized power relative to assumptions. All deviations, counts, and logs are archived in the evidence bundle.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator (not executed here). All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification; see the reproducibility paragraph and execution manifest for explicit artifact paths and hashes.

Preregistration: study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29 (preregistration SHA‑256 = aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a). Representative artifact hashes included in the evidence bundle: execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = fe9b93ef5cc5a237a3361f18f45fabf14cd23a1c679556f65477f9f681915d02; execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 5a822e787302a0b3bb03a86a81b20564a44e2636731f853f9d45ac12e4876cc8; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 8fb135cec541cbe0b14f16125db33154a41460c49958427fe8e7f3e1f2abfece; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = 261ec80ea9343fccbcd0a62294f5382773770fd59d387dc9d749de50ca909b3e. The design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed in this archived run; that unexecuted arm means the originally preregistered two‑test Bonferroni familywise plan could not be fully applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
